questions.title: How doping makes semiconductors useful
questions.prompt: Explain what a semiconductor is, how doping creates n-type and p-type material, and why a p-n junction lets current flow mainly in one direction.

expectedConcepts.label: Band gap between insulator and conductor
Doping adds electrons (n) or holes (p)
Depletion region and forward/reverse bias

questions.modelAnswer: A semiconductor such as silicon has a small band gap, so its conductivity sits between metals and insulators and can be controlled. Doping with phosphorus adds free electrons (n-type); with boron it creates holes (p-type). Where they meet, carriers diffuse and recombine, leaving a depletion region with a built-in field. Forward bias shrinks that region and current flows; reverse bias widens it and blocks current — the diode, the basis of transistors.

questions.title: How a MOSFET transistor works
questions.prompt: Explain how a MOSFET transistor works as a switch, including the source, drain, gate and channel. Why are transistors the building blocks of logic gates and computer chips?

expectedConcepts.label: Source, drain, gate, insulating oxide
Gate voltage forms a conducting channel
On/off switches form logic gates; CMOS
Billions of tiny transistors per chip

questions.modelAnswer: A MOSFET, metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, has a source and a drain, two doped regions in a silicon substrate, separated by a region where the channel can form. Above that region sits the gate, separated from the silicon by a very thin insulating oxide layer, so almost no current flows into the gate. In an n-channel MOSFET, applying a positive gate voltage above the threshold creates an electric field that draws electrons to the surface, forming a conducting channel between source and drain: the switch is on. Remove the voltage and the channel disappears: the switch is off. Because a voltage controls a current with very little input power, transistors can represent binary ones and zeros and drive other transistors. CMOS pairs n-type and p-type transistors so that in steady state one of them is always off, which keeps static power low, and combinations form inverters, NAND gates and every other logic gate, then adders, memory and whole processors. Modern chips pack tens of billions of transistors with features only nanometres wide.

questions.title: Chip manufacturing and Moore's law
questions.prompt: Explain how computer chips are manufactured using photolithography on silicon wafers. What is Moore's law, why has it slowed down, and how is the industry responding?

expectedConcepts.label: Pure silicon wafers processed in cleanrooms
Light through a mask patterns photoresist; etch and deposit layers
Transistor count doubles about every two years
Physical limits, cost, heat; chiplets, 3D stacking, new transistors

questions.modelAnswer: Chips start as wafers sliced from a single crystal of ultra-pure silicon and are made in cleanrooms, because a speck of dust can ruin a circuit. Photolithography patterns each layer: the wafer is coated with light-sensitive photoresist, light is projected through a mask carrying the circuit pattern, the exposed resist is developed away, and the uncovered areas are etched, doped with ions, or covered with deposited material. Repeating this dozens of times builds transistors and the metal wiring above them; the smallest features need extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nanometres. Moore's law is Gordon Moore's observation that the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every two years, which held for decades and made computers cheaper and faster. It has slowed because features are approaching the size of atoms, leakage and heat limit performance, and each new factory costs billions. The industry responds with new transistor shapes like FinFETs and gate-all-around, 3D stacking, chiplets combined in one package, and specialised accelerators for AI.

questions.title: Superposition without the hype
questions.prompt: Explain quantum superposition accurately for a general audience, including what measurement does, and correct one common misconception.

expectedConcepts.label: State is a combination of basis states with amplitudes
Measurement gives one outcome with Born-rule probabilities
Not 'secretly in one state' / not 'trying all answers'

questions.modelAnswer: A quantum system's state can be a combination of basis states, each with a complex amplitude. Measurement yields one definite outcome, with probabilities given by the squared magnitudes of the amplitudes (Born rule), and the state afterwards is consistent with that outcome. Amplitudes can interfere, which is what makes quantum algorithms work. Misconception: a quantum computer does not simply 'try all answers at once' and read off the right one — useful algorithms must arrange interference so wrong answers cancel.

questions.title: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle
questions.prompt: Explain the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. What exactly can't be known together, why is it a property of nature rather than a limit of our instruments, and how does it relate to wave-particle duality?

expectedConcepts.label: Position and momentum can't both be sharply defined
Product of uncertainties >= h-bar / 2
Not a measurement flaw; follows from waves
Wave packets: localised waves need many wavelengths

questions.modelAnswer: The uncertainty principle says certain pairs of properties, most famously position and momentum, can't both have sharply defined values at the same time. The more precisely a particle's position is defined, the more spread out its momentum must be, and vice versa: the product of the two uncertainties is at least h-bar over 2, Planck's reduced constant divided by two. It isn't a flaw in our instruments or just the measurement disturbing the particle; it comes from the wave nature of matter. A particle is described by a wave, and its momentum is tied to its wavelength. A wave with one precise wavelength stretches over all space, so its position is undefined; to build a wave packet localised in one place, you must add many wavelengths, which spreads the momentum. Planck's constant is tiny, so the effect is invisible for everyday objects but dominates for electrons. It explains why electrons don't collapse into the nucleus: confining one too tightly would give it a large momentum and energy.

questions.title: Quantum tunnelling and entanglement
questions.prompt: Explain quantum tunnelling and quantum entanglement in plain language. Give a real technology or natural process that depends on tunnelling, and explain why entanglement cannot be used to send messages faster than light.

expectedConcepts.label: A particle can cross a barrier it classically couldn't
Fusion in the Sun, flash memory, scanning tunnelling microscope
Entangled particles have correlated outcomes
Outcomes are random, so no faster-than-light messages

questions.modelAnswer: In quantum mechanics a particle is described by a wave function giving probabilities. When it meets an energy barrier it doesn't have enough energy to climb over, the wave doesn't stop dead; it decays inside the barrier, so if the barrier is thin there is a small probability of finding the particle on the other side. That's tunnelling. It lets hydrogen nuclei in the Sun fuse despite their repulsion, explains alpha decay, makes scanning tunnelling microscopes image individual atoms, and is how flash memory writes and erases charge; it is also a source of leakage in tiny transistors. Entanglement is when two particles share one quantum state, so measurements on them are correlated however far apart they are: measure one entangled photon's polarisation and you know what the other will show. Experiments testing Bell's inequalities show these correlations can't be explained by hidden pre-agreed values. But each individual outcome is random, so one side can't choose a result to encode a message; the correlation only appears when the results are compared over an ordinary, slower-than-light channel. That's why entanglement can't send information faster than light, though it is useful for quantum cryptography and computing.

questions.title: Stress-strain curves
questions.prompt: Explain what a stress–strain curve tells an engineer about a material. Cover elastic region, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and ductility.

expectedConcepts.label: Elastic region and Young's modulus
Yield strength = onset of permanent deformation
Ultimate tensile strength, necking, fracture

questions.modelAnswer: In a tensile test, stress (force per area) is plotted against strain (relative elongation). In the elastic region the curve is linear — its slope is Young's modulus — and the material returns to shape when unloaded. At the yield strength permanent plastic deformation begins. Stress rises with work hardening to the ultimate tensile strength, then necking localises deformation until fracture. Ductility is how much plastic strain occurs before fracture: steel stretches, glass doesn't.

questions.title: Crystal structures and defects in metals
questions.prompt: Explain how atoms are arranged in crystalline metals, and how defects such as dislocations and grain boundaries control strength. How do alloying, work hardening and heat treatment change a metal's properties?

expectedConcepts.label: Atoms in repeating lattices (FCC, BCC)
Plastic deformation by dislocations moving
Grain boundaries block dislocations
Alloying, work hardening, heat treatment

questions.modelAnswer: In a crystalline metal, atoms sit in a regular repeating lattice, such as face-centred cubic in aluminium and copper or body-centred cubic in iron at room temperature. Real crystals contain defects, and they control mechanical properties. Metals deform permanently not by whole planes of atoms sliding at once, which would need enormous force, but by dislocations, line defects that glide through the lattice one row of bonds at a time. So anything that obstructs dislocation motion makes a metal stronger but usually less ductile. A metal is made of many crystals, or grains, and grain boundaries block dislocations, so finer grains mean higher strength. Alloying adds atoms of a different size that distort the lattice and pin dislocations; carbon in iron makes steel. Work hardening, such as bending or rolling cold metal, multiplies and tangles dislocations, making it harder. Heat treatment changes the microstructure: annealing lets dislocations and grains rearrange, softening the metal, while quenching steel traps carbon in hard martensite, which is then tempered to reduce brittleness.

questions.title: Polymers and composite materials
questions.prompt: Explain what polymers are and the difference between thermoplastics and thermosets. Then explain composite materials such as carbon fibre reinforced plastic, and why they are used in aircraft and sports equipment.

expectedConcepts.label: Long chains of repeating monomers
Thermoplastics remelt; thermosets are cross-linked
Fibres in a matrix combine properties
High strength-to-weight for aircraft, bikes, rackets

questions.modelAnswer: A polymer is a very long chain molecule made by linking many small repeating units called monomers: ethene becomes polyethylene, for example. Thermoplastics such as polyethylene, PET and nylon have chains held together by weaker forces between them, so they soften when heated and can be remoulded and often recycled. Thermosets such as epoxy and the resin in old phone casings have chains cross-linked by strong covalent bonds into a network, so once cured they don't melt; they char instead, which makes them rigid and heat-resistant but hard to recycle. A composite combines two materials to get properties neither has alone, typically strong fibres embedded in a matrix that holds them in place and spreads the load. In carbon fibre reinforced plastic, stiff, strong carbon fibres carry the load and an epoxy matrix binds them, giving a strength-to-weight ratio far better than steel. That's why it is used in aircraft such as the Boeing 787, saving fuel, and in racing bikes, tennis rackets and Formula 1 cars. Drawbacks are cost, difficult repair and recycling, and weakness in directions without fibres.

questions.title: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonds
questions.prompt: Explain the main types of chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic. How does electronegativity decide which one forms, and how do bond types explain properties such as melting point and electrical conductivity?

expectedConcepts.label: Ionic: electron transfer, ions held by electrostatic attraction
Covalent: shared electron pairs, polar bonds
Metallic: cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
Electronegativity difference decides the bond type

questions.modelAnswer: Atoms bond to reach more stable electron arrangements. In an ionic bond, an electron moves from a metal to a non-metal, as from sodium to chlorine, forming ions held together by strong electrostatic attraction in a lattice: high melting points, and conductive when molten or dissolved, because the ions can move. In a covalent bond, non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons; if their electronegativities differ, the sharing is unequal and the bond is polar, as in water. Metallic bonding is a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, which explains why metals conduct electricity and can be bent without breaking. A large electronegativity difference favours ionic bonding and a small one favours covalent. Small covalent molecules have weak forces between molecules and low melting points, while giant covalent structures such as diamond are very hard.

questions.title: Acids, bases and the pH scale
questions.prompt: Explain what acids and bases are, how the pH scale works, and the difference between a strong and a weak acid. Give everyday examples and explain what a buffer does.

expectedConcepts.label: Acids donate protons (H+), bases accept them
pH is logarithmic; 7 is neutral
Strong acids dissociate fully, weak ones partially
Buffers resist pH change

questions.modelAnswer: In the Bronsted-Lowry view, an acid donates a proton (a hydrogen ion) and a base accepts one. pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen-ion concentration, so each step of 1 is a factor of ten; at 25 degrees Celsius pure water is 7 (neutral), below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic. A strong acid such as hydrochloric acid dissociates almost completely in water, while a weak acid such as acetic acid in vinegar dissociates only partially, so at the same concentration it has a higher pH. Lemon juice and vinegar are acidic; baking soda and soap are basic. A buffer, a weak acid mixed with its conjugate base, resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added; blood is kept near pH 7.4 by the carbonic acid and bicarbonate buffer.

questions.title: Reaction rates, activation energy and catalysts
questions.prompt: Explain what controls the rate of a chemical reaction using collision theory. Cover concentration, temperature, surface area and activation energy, and explain how a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

expectedConcepts.label: Particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation
Concentration, pressure, temperature, surface area
Activation energy is the minimum energy needed
A catalyst offers a lower-energy pathway and is regenerated

questions.modelAnswer: Particles react only when they collide with at least the activation energy and in a suitable orientation. Higher concentration, or higher pressure for gases, means more collisions per second. Greater surface area, a powder instead of a lump, exposes more particles to collisions. Higher temperature makes particles move faster and, more importantly, gives a much larger fraction of collisions enough energy, so rates often rise steeply with temperature. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed; it is regenerated at the end, so it is not used up, and it does not change the position of an equilibrium. Enzymes are biological catalysts, and a car's catalytic converter is an everyday example.

questions.title: Chemical equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle
questions.prompt: Explain dynamic chemical equilibrium and Le Chatelier's principle. Use an example such as the Haber process to show how changing concentration, pressure or temperature shifts the equilibrium.

expectedConcepts.label: Forward and reverse reactions at equal rates
The system shifts to oppose a change
Haber process: nitrogen + hydrogen <=> ammonia
Pressure favours fewer gas molecules; temperature and exothermic reactions

questions.modelAnswer: In a closed system, a reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium when the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant even though both reactions continue. Le Chatelier's principle says that if conditions change, the equilibrium shifts to partly oppose the change. In the Haber process, nitrogen plus three hydrogen form two ammonia, and the forward reaction is exothermic. Adding nitrogen or removing ammonia shifts the equilibrium to the right. Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, four on the left versus two on the right, so it raises the ammonia yield. Lower temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction and also raises the yield, but makes the reaction slow, so industry compromises at about 400 to 450 degrees Celsius and around 200 atmospheres with an iron catalyst. The catalyst helps reach equilibrium faster but does not shift it.

questions.title: Oxidation and reduction
questions.prompt: Explain oxidation and reduction. Define them in terms of electrons and oxidation states, and use examples such as rusting and batteries to show why the two always happen together.

expectedConcepts.label: Oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain (OIL RIG)
Electrons lost by one species are gained by another
Rusting: iron oxidised, oxygen reduced
Batteries: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode

questions.modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, which raises an element's oxidation state; reduction is the gain of electrons, which lowers it: OIL RIG, oxidation is loss, reduction is gain. Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another, so oxidation and reduction always happen together, which is why the reactions are called redox. In rusting, iron is oxidised to iron ions while oxygen is reduced, with water involved, forming hydrated iron oxide. Salt water speeds this up, and a zinc coating (galvanising) protects iron because zinc is oxidised first. In a battery the redox reaction is split in two: oxidation at the anode releases electrons that flow through the external circuit to the cathode, where reduction takes place, so chemical energy becomes electrical energy.

questions.title: The periodic table and its trends
questions.prompt: Explain how the periodic table is organised by atomic number, groups and periods. Describe the trends in atomic radius, ionisation energy and reactivity, and explain them using electron shells.

expectedConcepts.label: Atomic number; groups share outer electrons; periods are shells
Radius shrinks across a period, grows down a group
Ionisation energy and electronegativity rise across, fall down
Alkali metals more reactive down; halogens less reactive down

questions.modelAnswer: The periodic table orders elements by atomic number, the number of protons. Elements in the same column, a group, have the same number of outer (valence) electrons, so they behave similarly: group 1 alkali metals, group 17 halogens, group 18 noble gases with full shells that rarely react. Each row, a period, corresponds to filling a new electron shell. Across a period, the nuclear charge increases while electrons go into the same shell, so atoms get smaller, and ionisation energy, the energy needed to remove an electron, and electronegativity both increase. Down a group, each element adds a shell, outer electrons are farther away and more shielded by inner electrons, so atoms get bigger and ionisation energy falls. That explains reactivity: alkali metals react by losing an electron, so they get more reactive down the group, with caesium more violent than lithium; halogens react by gaining one, so they get less reactive down the group, with fluorine the most reactive.

questions.title: The mole and stoichiometry
questions.prompt: Explain what a mole is and why chemists use it, including Avogadro's number and molar mass. Then explain how a balanced equation lets you calculate the amounts of reactants and products, including the limiting reagent.

expectedConcepts.label: A mole is 6.022 x 10^23 particles
Molar mass in grams per mole
Balanced equations give mole ratios
Limiting reagent runs out first

questions.modelAnswer: Atoms are far too small to count individually, so chemists count them in moles. One mole is Avogadro's number, about 6.022 times 10 to the 23 particles, chosen so that the molar mass of a substance in grams per mole equals its relative atomic or formula mass: one mole of carbon-12 is 12 grams, and one mole of water is about 18 grams. A balanced equation tells you the ratio in which particles react, and therefore moles. In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen to make two moles of water, and atoms are conserved on both sides. To find how much product you get, convert masses to moles, use the mole ratio, and convert back to mass. If reactants are not in the exact ratio, the one that runs out first is the limiting reagent: it determines how much product forms, and the other reactant is left in excess.

questions.title: Organic chemistry and functional groups
questions.prompt: Explain why carbon forms so many compounds, the difference between alkanes, alkenes and alkynes, and what functional groups such as alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters are. Give everyday examples.

expectedConcepts.label: Carbon forms four bonds, chains and rings
Alkanes single, alkenes double, alkynes triple bonds
Functional groups decide reactions
Ethanol, vinegar, fruity esters, plastics

questions.modelAnswer: Carbon forms four covalent bonds and bonds strongly to other carbon atoms, so it builds long chains, branches and rings, giving millions of compounds; that's organic chemistry. Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes, such as methane in natural gas, have only single bonds and are saturated. Alkenes, such as ethene, have a carbon-carbon double bond, which makes them more reactive and lets them join into polymers like polyethylene. Alkynes have a triple bond. A functional group is the reactive part of a molecule that largely decides how it behaves. Alcohols have an OH (hydroxyl) group, like ethanol in drinks and hand sanitiser. Carboxylic acids have a COOH group and are weak acids, like acetic acid in vinegar. An alcohol and a carboxylic acid react to form an ester and water; esters often smell fruity and are used in flavourings and perfumes, while the same reaction joined into chains makes polyester.

questions.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
questions.prompt: Explain exothermic and endothermic reactions in terms of breaking and making bonds. What is enthalpy change, what does an energy profile diagram show, and what are everyday examples of each type?

expectedConcepts.label: Exothermic releases heat; endothermic absorbs it
Breaking bonds takes energy; forming bonds releases it
Enthalpy change, delta H negative for exothermic
Combustion, hand warmers; cold packs, photosynthesis

questions.modelAnswer: In every reaction, bonds in the reactants break and new bonds form in the products. Breaking a bond always takes energy, and forming a bond always releases energy. If forming the new bonds releases more energy than breaking the old ones took, the extra is given out to the surroundings, usually as heat, and the reaction is exothermic: the surroundings get hotter. If breaking bonds takes more energy than forming releases, the reaction absorbs energy and is endothermic: the surroundings get colder. Enthalpy change, delta H, is the heat exchanged at constant pressure: negative for exothermic reactions and positive for endothermic ones. An energy profile diagram plots energy along the reaction: products lower than reactants for exothermic, higher for endothermic, with a hump in between showing the activation energy. Exothermic examples include combustion, respiration and hand warmers; endothermic examples include photosynthesis, thermal decomposition, and instant cold packs that dissolve ammonium nitrate.

questions.title: Intermolecular forces and states of matter
questions.prompt: Explain intermolecular forces such as London dispersion forces, dipole-dipole interactions and hydrogen bonding. How do they explain boiling points, and why does water have such unusual properties?

expectedConcepts.label: Dispersion, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding
Forces between molecules, weaker than bonds within
Stronger forces mean higher boiling points
Hydrogen bonds give water high boiling point, ice floats

questions.modelAnswer: Intermolecular forces act between molecules and are much weaker than the covalent bonds within them. Boiling or melting a molecular substance only overcomes these forces; the molecules themselves stay intact. London dispersion forces come from temporary dipoles as electron clouds fluctuate; every molecule has them, and they grow with molecular size, which is why larger alkanes have higher boiling points. Polar molecules also attract each other through permanent dipole-dipole forces. Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong dipole attraction when hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine and is attracted to a lone pair on another such atom. The stronger the forces, the more energy is needed to separate molecules, so the higher the boiling point. Water is unusual because each molecule can form several hydrogen bonds: it boils at 100 degrees Celsius, far higher than similar-sized molecules like methane; it has high surface tension and heat capacity; and ice is less dense than liquid water because hydrogen bonds lock it into an open lattice, so ice floats.

questions.title: The gas laws and the ideal gas equation
questions.prompt: Explain the relationships between pressure, volume and temperature of a gas, including Boyle's law and Charles's law, and the ideal gas equation PV = nRT. Use kinetic theory to explain why they hold.

expectedConcepts.label: Boyle: P inversely proportional to V at constant T
Charles: V proportional to absolute temperature
PV = nRT
keywords: p v equals n r t

expectedConcepts.label: Kinetic theory: collisions with walls create pressure

questions.modelAnswer: Gas pressure comes from countless molecules colliding with the container walls; temperature measures their average kinetic energy. Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume, so halving the volume of a syringe doubles the pressure, because the same molecules hit the walls twice as often. Charles's law: at constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature in kelvin, so a balloon shrinks in the freezer, because slower molecules need less space to exert the same pressure. Gay-Lussac's law adds that at constant volume, pressure rises with temperature, which is why aerosol cans warn against heat. All of these combine into the ideal gas equation, PV = nRT, where n is the number of moles and R is the gas constant, 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin. Temperatures must be in kelvin. Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature, when molecular size and attractions start to matter.

questions.title: Newton's three laws of motion
questions.prompt: Explain Newton's three laws of motion with an everyday example for each. What does F = ma tell us, and why do objects in space keep moving without an engine?

expectedConcepts.label: First law: inertia, constant velocity without net force
Second law: F = ma
Third law: equal and opposite forces on different bodies
Everyday examples: seatbelts, pushing a cart, rockets

questions.modelAnswer: First law: an object stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity unless a net force acts on it. This is inertia; it's why passengers lurch forward when a car brakes and need seatbelts. Second law: the net force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma, so the same push accelerates an empty shopping cart more than a full one, and doubling the force doubles the acceleration. Third law: forces come in pairs; if A pushes B, B pushes A with an equal and opposite force, acting on different bodies, which is why a swimmer pushes water backwards to move forwards and a rocket pushes exhaust gas back to accelerate. In space there is almost no friction or air resistance, so no net force acts to slow a probe down; by the first law it keeps coasting, and engines are needed only to change its velocity.

questions.title: Work, energy and conservation of energy
questions.prompt: Explain work, kinetic energy and potential energy, and the law of conservation of energy. Use a roller coaster or a falling ball as an example, and explain where the energy goes when friction is present.

expectedConcepts.label: Work = force times distance moved in the force's direction
Kinetic (1/2 mv^2) and potential (mgh) energy
Energy is conserved, only converted
Friction turns mechanical energy into heat

questions.modelAnswer: Work is done when a force moves something: work equals force times the distance moved in the direction of the force, measured in joules, and it transfers energy. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, one half m v squared, so doubling speed quadruples it. Gravitational potential energy is stored energy due to height, m g h. The law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted between forms, so the total stays constant in a closed system. On a roller coaster, the chain lift does work to raise the car, storing potential energy at the top; as the car drops, potential energy turns into kinetic energy, and as it climbs the next hill, back into potential energy. With friction and air resistance, some mechanical energy turns into heat and sound, which is why each hill must be lower than the first and the ride eventually needs brakes or another lift.

questions.title: Momentum and collisions
questions.prompt: Explain momentum and the conservation of momentum. Compare elastic and inelastic collisions, and explain how airbags and crumple zones reduce injuries using impulse.

expectedConcepts.label: Momentum = mass x velocity, a vector
Total momentum is conserved without external forces
Elastic conserves kinetic energy; inelastic does not
Impulse: longer stopping time means smaller force

questions.modelAnswer: Momentum is mass times velocity, p = mv, and it is a vector, so direction matters. If no external force acts on a system, its total momentum is conserved: the total before a collision equals the total after, which is why a gun recoils and two skaters pushing apart move off in opposite directions. In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved, as with billiard balls, approximately; in an inelastic collision some kinetic energy turns into heat, sound and deformation, and in a perfectly inelastic one the objects stick together, while momentum is still conserved. Impulse, force times time, equals the change in momentum. In a crash, the car's occupants must lose the same momentum whatever happens, so airbags, seatbelts and crumple zones increase the time over which they stop, which reduces the force on the body and therefore injuries.

questions.title: Voltage, current, resistance and Ohm's law
questions.prompt: Explain voltage, current and resistance, Ohm's law, and electrical power. Compare series and parallel circuits, and explain why houses are wired in parallel.

expectedConcepts.label: Voltage pushes, current flows, resistance opposes
V = IR and P = VI
Series shares current; parallel shares voltage
Parallel wiring: independent appliances at full voltage

questions.modelAnswer: Voltage, or potential difference, is the energy given to each unit of charge, the push that drives it around a circuit, measured in volts. Current is the rate of flow of charge, in amperes. Resistance, in ohms, opposes the current. Ohm's law links them: V = IR, so for a fixed resistance, doubling the voltage doubles the current. Electrical power is P = VI, the rate of energy transfer in watts. In a series circuit, components form one loop: the same current flows through each, the voltages add up, and if one bulb fails, everything stops. In a parallel circuit, each component has its own branch across the supply: each gets the full voltage, the currents add up, and components work independently. That's why houses are wired in parallel: every appliance gets the full mains voltage and can be switched on or off without affecting the others.

questions.title: Electromagnetism and induction
questions.prompt: Explain how electricity and magnetism are connected. Cover the magnetic field around a current, how electric motors work, and how electromagnetic induction makes generators and transformers possible.

expectedConcepts.label: A current creates a magnetic field; electromagnets
Force on a current in a field turns a motor
Changing magnetic field induces a voltage (Faraday)
Generators and transformers (AC only)

questions.modelAnswer: An electric current creates a magnetic field around the wire; coiling the wire concentrates the field, making an electromagnet that can be switched on and off. A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force, and in an electric motor that force acts on a coil in opposite directions on each side, making it rotate; a commutator or the drive electronics keep reversing the current so it keeps spinning. The reverse effect is electromagnetic induction, discovered by Faraday: a changing magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage in it. A generator spins a coil in a magnetic field, or a magnet inside a coil, converting mechanical energy to electricity. A transformer uses alternating current in one coil to create a changing field in an iron core, which induces a voltage in a second coil; the ratio of turns steps the voltage up for efficient long-distance transmission and down for homes. Transformers only work with alternating current, because a steady current doesn't change the field.

questions.title: Waves, sound and the Doppler effect
questions.prompt: Explain what a wave is, the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves, and how wavelength, frequency and speed are related. Then explain the Doppler effect with an example.

expectedConcepts.label: Waves transfer energy, not matter
Transverse vs longitudinal
Speed = frequency x wavelength
Doppler: pitch rises as the source approaches

questions.modelAnswer: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from place to place without transferring matter; the particles of the medium just oscillate around fixed positions. In a transverse wave, like a wave on a rope or light, the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of travel. In a longitudinal wave, like sound, the oscillation is along the direction of travel, producing compressions and rarefactions in the air. Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: frequency is how many waves pass per second, in hertz, and wavelength is the distance between peaks. The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency when the source and observer move relative to each other: as an ambulance approaches, its sound waves are squashed together, so you hear a higher pitch; as it moves away, they are stretched, so the pitch drops. The same effect shifts light from receding galaxies towards red, which is evidence that the universe is expanding, and radar speed guns use it too.

questions.title: The laws of thermodynamics and entropy
questions.prompt: Explain the first and second laws of thermodynamics in simple terms. What is entropy, why can no heat engine be 100 percent efficient, and how does a refrigerator move heat from cold to hot?

expectedConcepts.label: First law: energy is conserved (heat + work)
Second law: heat flows hot to cold; entropy increases
Heat engines must reject some heat
Refrigerators use work to pump heat

questions.modelAnswer: The first law is conservation of energy: the change in a system's internal energy equals the heat added to it minus the work it does. You can't get energy for nothing. The second law says heat flows naturally from hot to cold, never the reverse on its own; equivalently, the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Entropy measures how many microscopic arrangements match a system's state, often described loosely as disorder. A heat engine, such as a car engine or power station, turns some heat from a hot source into work, but it must dump the rest as waste heat into a colder sink, so no engine can be 100 percent efficient; the Carnot limit, one minus the cold temperature over the hot temperature in kelvin, sets the maximum. A refrigerator is a heat pump run in reverse: a compressor does work on a refrigerant, which absorbs heat inside the fridge as it evaporates and releases it outside as it condenses. Moving heat from cold to hot is allowed, but only by doing work.

questions.title: Special relativity basics
questions.prompt: Explain the two postulates of special relativity and their consequences: time dilation, length contraction and E = mc squared. Give a real-world example where these effects matter.

expectedConcepts.label: Same laws in all inertial frames; constant speed of light
Moving clocks run slow; lengths contract
E = mc^2: mass is a form of energy
GPS satellites, muons, particle accelerators

questions.modelAnswer: Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in every inertial, non-accelerating frame, and the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, whatever their motion. To keep light's speed constant, space and time must adjust. Time dilation: a clock moving relative to you runs slow by the factor gamma, which only becomes noticeable near the speed of light. Length contraction: a moving object is shorter along its direction of motion. Mass and energy are equivalent, E = mc squared, so a tiny mass corresponds to a huge energy, as in nuclear reactors and the Sun. Real examples: muons created by cosmic rays high in the atmosphere live long enough to reach the ground only because of time dilation, and GPS satellites must correct their clocks for relativity; without corrections, which also include general relativity's gravitational effect, position errors would grow by kilometres per day. Particle accelerators rely on these effects every day.

questions.title: What a derivative really means
questions.prompt: Explain what a derivative is, both as a rate of change and as the slope of a tangent line. Describe how it is defined using limits, give real-world examples, and explain how derivatives help find maximum and minimum values.

expectedConcepts.label: Instantaneous rate of change
Slope of the tangent line
Limit of the difference quotient
Derivative is zero at a max or min

questions.modelAnswer: A derivative measures how fast one quantity changes with respect to another at a single instant. If position depends on time, its derivative is velocity, and the derivative of velocity is acceleration. Geometrically, the derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent line to the curve there. It is defined with a limit: take the average rate of change between x and x plus h, that is f of x plus h minus f of x, divided by h, and let h approach zero. For example, the derivative of x squared is 2x, so at x equals 3 the curve rises 6 units per unit of x. Real-world uses include speed from distance, marginal cost in economics, and growth rates. At a smooth maximum or minimum, the tangent is flat, so the derivative is zero; setting the derivative to zero and checking the sign of the second derivative finds optimal values, such as the dimensions that minimise material for a can, and gradient descent in machine learning follows derivatives downhill.

questions.title: Integrals and the fundamental theorem of calculus
questions.prompt: Explain what an integral is as the area under a curve and as an accumulated total. How does the fundamental theorem of calculus connect integration and differentiation? Give practical examples.

expectedConcepts.label: Area under a curve / accumulation
Limit of sums of thin rectangles
Integration reverses differentiation; antiderivatives
Distance from velocity, work, probability

questions.modelAnswer: A definite integral adds up a quantity that changes continuously. Geometrically, it is the signed area under a curve between two points. You can picture it as splitting the area into thin rectangles, adding their areas, and taking the limit as the rectangles become infinitely thin; that limit of sums is the Riemann integral. The same idea is accumulation: integrate velocity over time and you get distance travelled; integrate a power reading over time and you get energy used. The fundamental theorem of calculus connects integration and differentiation as inverse operations: if F is an antiderivative of f, meaning F's derivative is f, then the integral of f from a to b equals F of b minus F of a. So instead of summing rectangles, you find an antiderivative; for example, the integral of 2x from 0 to 3 is 3 squared minus 0 squared, which is 9. Integrals also give volumes, work done by a varying force, and probabilities as areas under a probability density curve.

questions.title: Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.prompt: Explain conditional probability and Bayes' theorem. Use the example of a medical test with a small false positive rate for a rare disease, and explain why a positive result may still mean the disease is unlikely.

expectedConcepts.label: P(A given B): probability once B is known
Bayes: update a prior with evidence
Base rate: rare disease means many false positives
Working through counts gives the answer

questions.modelAnswer: Conditional probability, P(A given B), is the probability of A once we know B happened, and equals P(A and B) divided by P(B). Bayes' theorem reverses the condition: P(A given B) equals P(B given A) times P(A), divided by P(B). In words, start with a prior belief P(A), multiply by how likely the evidence is if A is true, and normalise to get the posterior. Take a disease that 1 in 1,000 people have, and a test that detects 99 percent of cases with a 1 percent false positive rate. Out of 100,000 people, 100 have the disease and about 99 test positive; of the 99,900 healthy people, about 999 also test positive. So of roughly 1,098 positives, only 99 are sick, about 9 percent. Because the disease is rare, false positives from the large healthy group outnumber the true positives; ignoring this is the base rate fallacy. This is why positive screening results are confirmed with a second, more specific test.

questions.title: Matrices, eigenvectors and eigenvalues
questions.prompt: Explain what a matrix does as a linear transformation, and what eigenvectors and eigenvalues are. Give an intuitive picture, and describe where they are used, such as PCA or Google's PageRank.

expectedConcepts.label: A matrix is a linear transformation: rotate, stretch, shear
Eigenvectors keep their direction; eigenvalue is the scale factor
PCA, PageRank, vibrations, stability
Natural axes of the transformation; repeated application

questions.modelAnswer: A matrix represents a linear transformation: multiplying a vector by it rotates, stretches, shears or reflects the vector, while keeping straight lines straight and the origin fixed. Most vectors change direction under the transformation, but some special vectors only get stretched or shrunk along their own line: these are eigenvectors, and the factor by which each is scaled is its eigenvalue, so A v equals lambda v. Intuitively, eigenvectors are the natural axes of the transformation: in their coordinates the matrix just scales each axis. They matter when you apply a transformation repeatedly, because the direction with the largest eigenvalue comes to dominate. Principal component analysis finds eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix: the top ones are the directions of greatest variance, used to reduce dimensions. Google's original PageRank is the dominant eigenvector of the web's link matrix, found by repeated multiplication (power iteration). Engineers also use eigenvalues for vibration modes and to check whether systems are stable.

questions.title: Proof by mathematical induction
questions.prompt: Explain proof by mathematical induction using the domino analogy. Walk through proving that the sum of the first n natural numbers is n times n plus one over two, and mention where induction appears in computer science.

expectedConcepts.label: Base case and inductive step
Domino analogy
Sum formula proof
Recursion and loop invariants

questions.modelAnswer: Induction proves that a statement holds for every natural number in two steps. The base case shows it is true for the first value, usually n = 1. The inductive step shows that if it is true for some n, the inductive hypothesis, then it must also be true for n + 1. Like dominoes: the first one falls, and each falling domino knocks over the next, so they all fall. Example: claim 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2. Base case: for n = 1, the left side is 1 and the right side is 1 times 2 over 2, which is 1. Inductive step: assume the formula holds for n. Then the sum up to n + 1 equals n(n + 1)/2 plus (n + 1), which is (n + 1)(n + 2)/2, exactly the formula with n + 1 in place of n. So it holds for all n. In computer science, the same reasoning proves recursive functions correct, where the base case and recursive case mirror the proof, and proves loops correct using loop invariants.

questions.title: Mean, median, variance and the normal distribution
questions.prompt: Explain the mean, median and mode, and when the median is a better summary than the mean. Then explain standard deviation, the normal distribution, and the 68-95-99.7 rule.

expectedConcepts.label: Mean, median, mode
Median resists outliers and skew
Variance and standard deviation measure spread
Normal distribution and 68-95-99.7

questions.modelAnswer: The mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are; the median is the middle value when they are sorted; the mode is the most common value. The mean uses every value, but outliers pull it: if a billionaire walks into a cafe, the mean income in the room jumps while the median barely moves. So for skewed data such as incomes or house prices, the median is a better summary of a typical value. Spread is measured by variance, the average squared distance from the mean, and its square root, the standard deviation, which is in the original units. Many measurements, such as heights or measurement errors, roughly follow the normal distribution: a symmetric bell curve centred on the mean. For a normal distribution, about 68 percent of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95 percent within two, and about 99.7 percent within three, so a value three standard deviations away is unusual.

questions.title: Why the nanoscale is different
questions.prompt: Explain what the nanoscale is and why materials behave differently at that size. Cover the surface-area-to-volume ratio, quantum effects such as quantum dots, and examples of nanotechnology in everyday products.

expectedConcepts.label: 1 to 100 nanometres; a nanometre is a billionth of a metre
High surface-area-to-volume ratio boosts reactivity
Quantum confinement: size-dependent colour
Sunscreen, silver antibacterial, displays, chips

questions.modelAnswer: The nanoscale is roughly 1 to 100 nanometres; a nanometre is a billionth of a metre, about the width of ten hydrogen atoms in a row, and a human hair is around 80,000 nanometres thick. Two things change at this scale. First, the surface-area-to-volume ratio becomes huge: a much larger fraction of atoms sits on the surface, so nanoparticles are far more reactive and make excellent catalysts. Gold, unreactive in bulk, becomes catalytic as nanoparticles. Second, quantum effects appear: in quantum dots, electrons are confined in a tiny space, so the energy gaps, and therefore the colour of light they emit, depend on particle size, which is used in QLED displays. Everyday examples include zinc oxide and titanium dioxide nanoparticles in clear sunscreens, silver nanoparticles in antibacterial coatings, and transistors in modern chips with features only tens of nanometres across. Open questions include the health and environmental effects of some nanoparticles, so they are studied and regulated carefully.

questions.title: Graphene and carbon nanotubes
questions.prompt: Explain what graphene and carbon nanotubes are, how their structure relates to graphite, and why they have remarkable strength and conductivity. What applications are realistic, and what has held them back?

expectedConcepts.label: One-atom-thick hexagonal carbon sheet; rolled into tubes
Very strong, light, excellent conductor
Composites, batteries, sensors, electronics
Hard to manufacture at scale and quality; no band gap

questions.modelAnswer: Graphite is made of stacked sheets of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons. A single one-atom-thick sheet is graphene, first isolated in 2004 by peeling graphite with sticky tape, work that won a Nobel Prize. A carbon nanotube is like a sheet of graphene rolled into a seamless cylinder a few nanometres wide. Each carbon is strongly bonded to three neighbours in the plane, giving exceptional tensile strength and stiffness for very low weight, while the remaining electron of each atom is delocalised across the sheet, so graphene conducts electricity and heat extremely well; nanotubes can be metallic or semiconducting depending on how they are rolled. Realistic applications today are as additives: stronger, lighter composites in sports equipment and aerospace, conductive coatings, battery electrodes and sensors. What has held them back is manufacturing high-quality material cheaply at scale, controlling defects, and the fact that graphene has no band gap, so it can't simply replace silicon in transistors.
